utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you, too. You may be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Also, go to the Defence team. I'm here with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, may it please Your Honour, my name is John Jones, and I appear on behalf of Naser Oric, with Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant, and Geoff Roberts, our case manager. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you and your team. I hear you've been exchanging bouquets of flowers before the sitting, the Prosecution and Defence. So what's the problem, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to raise this by way of preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I anticipated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as Your Honour is aware, obviously, there was an adjournment yesterday, and my understanding was that was because there were new documents or new matters which had come to light during the proofing of today's witness, and the purpose of the adjournment was to give the Prosecution time and to give us time, having been provided with these new documents or this new material, to be prepared for today. And my understanding is that a member of your staff in fact told the Prosecution to provide us as soon as possible with any new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those were my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It goes without saying that B/C/S versions of the document are following as well because my -- our legal assistant speaks B/C/S and, of course, Ms. Vidovic is at the end of a fax and she can see documents in B/C/S, so I think it was abundantly clear to everyone that if there was any problem with translation, then we should receive the B/C/S versions immediately, and then English as soon as that's available. As it turned out, we waited all day yesterday, all of this morning, and received no new proofing notes, no new documents. We actually phoned the Prosecution, we phoned their case manager, and said, Are there going to be new proving notes, are there going to be new documents? And the first we heard was around 1.45 today, as the whole team was pretty much on their way to court, that some documents had been left in our locker. Our legal assistant checked the locker at ten past 1.00 and the documents weren't there. So sometime after 1.10, perhaps at 1.30, they were delivered there. So not only is it less than one hour before today's sitting, but in fact it deprives us of any realistic opportunity of considering those document. As I say, we're just arriving at court with 10 or 20 minutes before today's hearing, and it's simply not possible for us to consider a series of documents which are going to be used with this witness in that space of time. Now, the difficulty now is that we've lost yesterday already. I'm really minded to apply for an adjournment to give us time to consider these documents seriously. One possibility, one possible solution, just because I don't think any of us want to lose any more time, is the solution which was adopted when I used a video exhibit of the Telering programme, which is that the Prosecution not deal with those documents today, and that gives us an opportunity at the first break, or even between now and the first break, to fax the documents to Sarajevo so my lead counsel can consider it, because the fact is I've taken this witness over from my lead counsel and I think we should have an opportunity for her to see the documents, which was also the point of having all of yesterday to deal with any of these matters. And then the Prosecution can deal with those documents tomorrow. There's also an added difficulty in that today we have an afternoon sitting and we're sitting in the morning tomorrow, and I would submit that that's all the more reason why the Prosecution should've have made every effort to get these documents to us as soon as possible, and that one hour before the hearing is unacceptable. That's what I'd have to say on that matter. I understand, and I raise it not because there's any linkage at all. On the contrary. In my submission, there's absolutely no linkage whatsoever between the two issues. But the Prosecution have been asking for the exhibits we intend to use with this witness. Now, the practice since October, since this trial started, has not been that we are under an obligation to provide physical copies of documents. It's been that we file an exhibit list for the witness. If it's the case of a video recording, then the practice has been that we provide a copy beforehand. On a number of occasions, or very few occasions, in fact, as a matter of courtesy, when the Prosecution have asked, we've provided copies of the documents. But in our submission, we're under no obligation to do so, and certainly not before examination-in-chief starts. It's one thing before cross-examination, and we're perfectly happy with providing documents before cross-examination, but there's -- there's a very important reason why we don't provide documents before examination-in-chief, and that is that the witness may give an account which is substantially different, as we've seen in this case, in some respects, from what they've said in prior statements. Our cross-examination, and the documents we intend to use, are based on our first assessment of what the witness is going to testify about. If that changes, then our use of exhibits can change dramatically. And if we're obliged to provide documents to the Prosecution before the witness even begins testifying, in the end, we'll end up disclosing documents which we don't even use, and in my submission, we're under no obligation under the Rules to disclose documents to the Prosecution, particularly when we -- as I say, we may not use them. In my submission, that's an entirely different issue, and my main point is really to express my deep dissatisfaction, given that yesterday was adjourned, that we're now facing possibly more delays due to this very, very late disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Of course, there's no doubt about it that you are in a different position than -- than the Prosecution, and that there are certainly two types of documents that one could envisage in relation to the role of the Defence during the examination of -- and cross-examination of a witness, and that's documents that you obviously know that you would be needing before the examination-in-chief starts, and documents that become necessary as the examination-in-chief progresses. It's obvious. I mean, you definitely have the Trial Chamber's understanding. But as far as the examination-in-chief is concerned, however, the Trial Chamber will certainly appreciate if any documents that you certainly intend to make use of, and you know that you will be making use of even before the examination-in-chief starts, you will make known and possibly give copies of -- to the Prosecution. I also understand that most of the documents that you have been supplied to you by the Prosecution itself, so at that point in time I don't think it's a case of supplying copies, but it will be -- to suffice if you just make a reference to the numbers. But let's leave it at that for the time being and see what Mr. Wubben has to say on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I just say on that matter, Your Honour, we would need further clarification of precisely what obligations we have before that's sort of set in stone, because there are issues of whether -- well, firstly, we wouldn't want any documents which we provide to the Prosecution to be used in proofing the witness, because then we're giving advance notice of points we're going to raise to the witness. It's one thing for the Prosecution to be prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I said you are in a different position --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- from the Prosecution, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But perhaps we can discuss that issue separately from this issue problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I will leave that issue aside, and we'll concentrate on whether the sitting should proceed or not in the first place. And if it does, on what basis, and how. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Patricia Sellers will address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Defence counsel. We have certainly taken Defence counsel's pleading with great seriousness, and we would like to say that he is in a position where the documents would have been much more beneficial had he received them last night. I will say that we continued to choose these documents and discover these documents until after closing hours, and then wanted to have them translated for our benefit to find out whether we would use them. That is by way of explanation, that is not by way of any excuse. I understand that these documents would have been delivered a bit earlier. Our translations completed at 12.00, and then we proceeded to get documents with translations to the Defence. Understanding that this might but the Defence in what is considered or termed an unreasonable position, the Prosecution would suggest that the new documents that now you have copies of both the original and the English translation for people like myself and I believe Mr. Jones who are not completely fluent in Bosnian, that they would not be used in today's part of the examination. Certainly, they were documents that I intended to use towards the latter part of the examination. That way Defence counsel certainly could look at the documents, convey any of their contents to lead counsel who, unfortunately, is not here, and there would be no prejudice on their behalf. Your Honours, if I just might say one thing concerning the second part of Defence counsel's argument that concerns documents that Defence provides to the Prosecution, I completely agree that there might be different circumstances. But I would like to underscore that the Prosecution's point of view is that documents that the Defence is more or less certain, they should be able to provide it. We have nine documents that are on your list that do not have ERN numbers that are basically letters from the prosecution courts -- different prosecution courts of Bosnia, which I would assume that you are going to use and that you do have in your possession. I would state in the very least, as a matter of courtesy, we would like to show these documents to our witness prior to taking the stand. In terms of obligation, I think we can look at the Trial Chamber's ruling when the trial began and just talk about the ability not in any manner to ambush either the Defence nor Prosecution witnesses. And certainly it's in that spirit that the Prosecution would like to convey that one possible, we would readily appreciate and accept Defence documents prior to the witness taking the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Two things to wind this discussion up. As regards the practice that should be adopted, I think we will come to that at some later point in time, when it is relevant and important and appropriate to discuss it. But I think the guiding principles ought to be more or less what has been stated. First, that those documents that you are more or less certain you would be making use of should be indicated, and other documents that the Prosecution may not be in possession of, in particular, as a minimum, out of courtesy, ought to be disclosed or made available to the Prosecution. That's as a matter of principle, but we'll come to that part of the discussion at some later point in time. As regards today, I think more or less the two positions have now converged. I take it that you will not be making use of these seven documents today, which basically meets you not halfway, it's more or less what you stated you would be happy with as a matter of last resort.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, we are discussing in a sort of a vacuum, because I would like to see these seven documents to see what is involved, because if we're talking of seven documents, each containing 40 pages, that's one thing; if we're talking of seven documents, each containing one page or a page and a half, it's another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's more a case of the latter, each containing a page and a half, a couple contain one or two pages. I believe Defence counsel does have the documents now. And basically we had put in our prior submission that would be entering -- submitting into evidence the attachment to the witness statement, and in that attachment were several documents that related to the Prosecutor in Srebrenica. We're now in possession of some other documents that relate to her, so in order to chronologically fill ut that submission that would have come through the attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In addition, may I ask you whether you have provided the Defence with the proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we provided the Defence with the proofing notes on, I believe, Monday. There were very few proofing notes because this witness certainly has indicated to us that there were very few changes to the statement, and I clearly expressed to Defence counsel in our e-mail the changes that the witness told us, including names, places or times. I would just like to state, if I could, in terms of proofing notes, the position of the Prosecutor is that the practice is certainly a practice that does vary, and anything that we believe is relevant to the Defence, that in any way would come in the way of ambushing them, we would convey to them. There are many things that a witness says that might be in addition but are not material or relevant, or merely expand upon what has been conveyed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Last but not least, could we have an indication of how long this witness will be in the witness box?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness will take today, and because of the nature we've been discussing, the documents, the witness should be finished within the first hour of tomorrow morning's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And cross-examination? Of course, on the proviso that you still haven't familiarised yourself with these seven documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I thought two and a half hours, probably maximum, two to two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the anticipation is that we should finish with this witness tomorrow? Because if it's one hour, plus two and a half, it's three and a half hours, which is within the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That will bring us to Friday. Friday, what's the position? Friday, the position is this: For the time being, there is an Extraordinary Plenary of the Judges scheduled for 1.30, which would mean that we would have to stop at about 1.00, 1.15, at the latest. That's number 1. If there is no Plenary session -- if there is no Plenary session, I will have an initial appearance at 2.15, which means that we could go on until quarter to 2.00, as per the usual time schedule. The next witness after this one, would you be able to finish with him in one day, or is he going to stay here the weekend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have got the information from the register -- from my legal officer that explains everything. All right. Shall we proceed with this witness and not waste more time, or lose more time, because we haven't certainly wasted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, because -- I was not aware of this, as you may have guessed, but I am put on notice by my legal secretary -- legal officer, that -- to make sure that you are aware that the Prosecution is not in a position to bring a witness on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't sure of the position, but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures in place for this witness. I just need a confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So good afternoon to you, Mr. Tankic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I proceed further, any further, although I already have an indication of this, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I also want to make sure that the sound level is comfortable. If it's not adequate or if it's too loud, too high, please tell us and we'll make the necessary adjustments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From now onwards, until you finish your testimony, if at any time there are problems with interpretation, particularly if interpretation is not reaching you, please draw our attention straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are about to start giving evidence, and so it is my duty, as the Presiding Judge in this trial, to welcome you. I welcome you on behalf of the Tribunal, but also on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, who comes from Denmark, who is sitting to my right, and Judge Albin Eser, who comes from Germany, sitting to my left. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. This is the trial against Naser Oric, and you are one of the witnesses that the Prosecution has summoned. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, and I will be very brief on this because of your background, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration; that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained on a piece of paper which is being handed to you now by Madam Usher. Please read that statement out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure you know. It's a very simple one. Ms. Sellers, for the Office of the Prosecutor and for the Prosecution, of course, will go first with her examination-in-chief, and she will then be followed by Mr. Jones who is co-counsel appearing for Naser Oric. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please state your record -- state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Izo Tankic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, is your ethnic origin Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you a graduate in law from the university of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you graduate in 1980?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In 1987, were you appointed as a judge to the High Court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you remain at the High Court in Tuzla until 1996?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have functions during that time period of investigating judge as well as judge?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During the years of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, specifically 1992 until 1996, did you serve in the armed forces in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you, therefore, a civilian in your work capacity at the High Court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber, what is the jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla, in 1992 and up until 1996?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The Tuzla High Court had jurisdiction over what was at the time the Tuzla district, which was established after the war had broken out. It had both first instance jurisdiction and the jurisdiction of a higher court. It applied all the criminal laws that were adopted from the former Yugoslavia in the area of its own district. The Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted, its general, special provisions, as well as the criminal code of the former socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The law on criminal procedure was adopted too which was applied throughout the former Yugoslavia. All of these laws and codes were adopted pursuant to a decision of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In addition to criminal jurisdiction, it had jurisdiction over litigations, jurisdiction as that of a high court. Its first instance jurisdiction was something that was a result of the existing laws, but it also prosecuted criminal matters in which sentences were passed of up to 10 years' imprisonment. I'm talking about first instance decisions. It handled appeals also, whenever decisions of the basic courts within the district were appealed. Needless to say, it had other tasks too, such as administrative litigation and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, prior to the outbreak of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, what was the geographical territory that the High Court in Tuzla covered in terms of how many municipalities?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: It was a large area in the north-east of Bosnia, Orasac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Zvornik, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Kladanj, Lukavac, Gracanica, Tuzla, Kalesija, Srebrenik, Banovici, Zivinice, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In terms of the subject matter jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla in 1992, prior to the autumn of 1992, did it try the cases in the Penal Code that were considered the most serious cases?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, if, when you say, serious cases, you mean cases where sentences passed might be over 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And the jurisdiction of lower courts or municipal courts, what types of crimes could they try?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: They tried crimes with sentences less than 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the Criminal Code originated from that of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like Mr. Tankic to be shown the Prosecution's first exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, do we need the entire code --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only going to go to certain segments of the code, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also have the code now on Sanction, and we'll be highlighting certain sections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at the first page of the code. Is this the Criminal Code that you've testified about in terms of the jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Criminal Code that was adopted at the republican level by decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask you to turn to page, in the English version, 43, and look at Article 113. Mr. Tankic, under Article 113, subparagraph 5, do you see that the code makes reference to military persons?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is it your understanding that under this Criminal Code, military persons, meaning soldiers in the military service, cadets at the military academy, junior officers on active duty, officers on active duty or military employees, reservists on military duty as servicemen, and a civilian person executing a certain military duty, came under the in personam jurisdiction of the High Tuzla Court in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did it mean that under the criminal law in the former socialist Yugoslavia, that military personnel could be tried for criminal matters in civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask us to turn to Article 142, on page 52 in the English version. Mr. Tankic, did the Criminal Code in the former Yugoslavia contain provisions that related to what we would call international crimes, such as crimes against humanity, genocide, or war crimes?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The Criminal Code contained so-called special provisions which, among other things, contained crimes against humanity and international law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I please draw your attention to Article 142 of the code. Is it your understanding that a war crime, a war crime against a civilian population that included, and I would ask you to look further down in that paragraph, a little more than midway, included acts of property confiscation, pillaging, illegal and self-will destruction, and stealing on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before the witness answers this question. I think you're trying to transform the witness into someone giving us legal advice or giving us a legal opinion. Article 142, once you're going to tender this code in evidence, Article 142 is there, we can read it, and it says what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I can assure you that nothing that is not included there is included, and nothing that is excluded is included.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That would certainly assist me, because I believe that we could go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But don't ask the witness to confirm to us what is the correct -- what interpretation, not even the word "interpretation," what is the correct interpretation of Article 142, what is included under 142. It's not for him to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I intend to ask the witness is whether this crime was incorporated under the jurisdiction of the court -- the High Court in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then ask him that question. Ask him to look at Article 142, ask him to confirm that Article 142, as we have it here in front of us, is the Article 142 that he is familiar with, and then proceed with the question as to whether that fell under the jurisdiction of his -- that particular court or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to highlight that under that Article 142, that there are specific acts that are certainly relevant to the matter before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, again, we don't need the witness to confirm that to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, you've heard Judge Agius's question. Could you confirm that Article 142, as incorporated in the Criminal Code, was within the jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask you to turn to page 53 and ask you a similar question as it pertains to Article 144 of the code, war crimes against prisoners of war. Was this also under the jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla prior to the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And as a general matter, the entire Criminal Code was part of the subject matter jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla. Will you confirm that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are serious crimes where the sentences envisaged there is over 10 years, and that's why the High Court has jurisdiction over these crimes, that's if you have in mind crimes against humanity or international law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you say these were serious crimes, could you please tell us what were the penalties for these types of international crimes, or the potential penalty for these crimes, under the code?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, the minimum was five years, as the maximum sentence, even a death penalty was envisaged, as well as alternatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tankic, was this Criminal Code applicable after the Republic of Bosnia declared its independence on the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This code was adopted by decree as a republican code.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that the Prosecution exhibit be given a P number and moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. What's the next -- the progressive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P496, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be Prosecution Exhibit P496. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tankic, between 1992 and 1996, did the jurisdiction of the High Court in Tuzla change in any manner? Was it modified?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: It changed after the district military courts had been set up, to try military personnel. There were no other changes in relation to any other types of crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was there any change in the geographical reach of the Tuzla court between 1992 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: After the war broke out, districts were set up, or rather, free territory. The High Court in Tuzla had jurisdiction over that area, and that area was substantially smaller than before the war. If you like, I can name the municipalities which existed between 1992 and 1996, which were included in the area over which the High Court had jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, please, would you inform the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, while -- before you start doing this, which I submit is a very important exercise, you can also tell us, perhaps, where these military courts were set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be getting to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The municipalities comprised by the Tuzla district were as follows: Kladanj, Banovici, Zivinice, Lukavac, Gracanica, Gradaca, parts of the Brcko municipality, Kalesija, Tuzla. Later on, municipalities were set up in Celici, Sapna, and Srebrenik. That was during the war. I believe I've listed all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like --

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I forgot Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber, what was the purpose of the creation of what you have called the district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Still during the peace period, our tradition was to have these special courts which tried only the cases against military persons, and we heard a short while ago what was the definition of military persons. So only when perpetrators of criminal offences were military persons, these military courts had jurisdiction over such cases. Due to that tradition, and due to the fact that the war broke out and there were many soldiers, we established this court. I believe it was towards the end of August when the law was adopted, and the courts started to operate in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Which persons could be brought before a district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Only military persons and exceptionally civilians in certain cases prescribed by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did that mean that military members and the certain civilians could be subjected to investigations, prosecutions, and judgements in the district military courts and no longer in the municipal or high courts that you spoke about earlier?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was much discussion regarding these jurisdictions, especially if you have as a core perpetrators, a civilian and a military person. There were specific rules applied to decide when a civilian court would have jurisdiction in these cases or when, alternatively, it would be under the jurisdiction only of the military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the August 13th, 1992 statutory order on district military courts?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I am generally familiar with the law, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is it your understanding that the district military court was established because of the situation of armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to show Prosecution Exhibit -- it has an ERN number of 00609188.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would like to ask you to look at Article 1. Does this cover the temporal jurisdiction of the court or a time period when the court -- district military court is established?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, only during the state of war or armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention now to Article 5, and the last square in Article 5. And is it your understanding that a district military court was established in Tuzla for the territory or district of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I please draw your attention now to Article 6 of the document. Mr. Tankic, is the fact that the district military court has jurisdiction over the criminal acts of military persons and of other civilians, did that mean that the High Court in Tuzla no longer exercised jurisdiction over the acts of military persons?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was now only under the jurisdiction of military courts if the perpetrators were military persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, could you now please look at Article 11 of the document before you. Did the jurisdiction of the district military court also include jurisdiction over prisoners of war for criminal acts that those prisoners might be accused of having committed?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. District military courts had jurisdiction over war prisoners if they committed criminal acts as war prisoners, and also they had jurisdiction over criminal acts against humanity and international law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you to look at Article 12, please, of the document. Was the district military court able to incorporate regulations that come from the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and the protocols that are annexed to the conventions?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This provision says so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I believe we are falling back to what I tried to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. There's a very thin line. I just have one or two other questions because I'm going toward the jurisdiction of the district military court, and so that can be more fully understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's always the risk of the witness either not understanding the question or having a different interpretation of a legal provision. What if he answers no? Then all of a sudden we have a problem. We've got a legal expert, because he's being asked to provide a legal opinion, giving an opinion which is the exact opposite of what is contained in the text that we are reading. I mean, please try to avoid that possibility, that eventuality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking you not to ask him to give opinion, unless it's the case of asking him for an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I believe it's his understanding, as having sat on one court, that he now no longer had jurisdiction when it came to certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm asking for his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, in addition to jurisdiction over the regulations to the Geneva Conventions, did the district military court also incorporate the Criminal Code from the former Yugoslavia that had come into -- promulgated in the Republic of Bosnia after the declaration of its independence?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like you to now look at Article 23 and tell me whether that reflects the incorporation of the Bosnian Criminal Code within the subject matter jurisdiction of the district military court.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Here the law on regular courts was accepted, which also regulates special issues regarding the operating of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could the articles that we've previously looked at in the Criminal Code, specifically Articles 141 through 143, could they be applied as part of the subject matter jurisdiction of the district military courts?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: If perpetrators were military persons, then the courts of first instance who had jurisdiction over such crimes were only military courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your attention to Article 27. And would it be your evidence that commanders of military units and military institutions had certain obligations in order to detain persons who committed criminal acts that came under the jurisdiction of the district military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need him to confirm what we can read in the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just move the text into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm expecting you to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I certainly wanted to. I wanted to highlight two other parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sort of interrupting you from time to time on the assumption that you will be tendering this in evidence. In fact, I have already given it a number myself in anticipation of the registrar telling me 497.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make certain points on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then very lastly, Article 29, does that concern also commanders, military commanders in the post of commander of the guard have certain obligations under the district military court, Mr. Tankic?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now ask for a P number and ask that this be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. P497.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P497, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, being the statutory order on district military courts is being tendered and marked and accepted as Prosecution Exhibit P497. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, how were the penalties determined for the crimes that came under the jurisdiction of the district military courts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Did he ever sit in the district military court?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: He has knowledge of this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's ask him that first, whether he has knowledge of how the district military courts worked out or reached its sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, could you respond to that question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: If he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he knows, obviously. I suppose that as an ex-judge in the civil courts, you know exactly how -- what the process or the procedure was in deciding what the penalty, what the punishment is, in each case. Are you aware or are you in a position to give us information as to how the district military courts did that, arrived at the quantum of the penalty or the punishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The civilian court and the military court applied the same laws. The only difference was who the perpetrator was. So my knowledge derives from the civilian court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would it be within your knowledge to say that the war crimes that we looked at previously concerning prisoners of war and concerning war crimes on civilians remained serious crimes in terms of penalty under the district military courts as they had when they were tried in the high courts of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the most serious crimes recognised by the Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, when did the district court in Tuzla come into being?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The military court?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The district military court, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: In September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you some questions, if you know, of how the district military court functioned. To your knowledge, did the district military court have a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had a district military prosecutor who acted at the district military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the district military court, to your knowledge, also have investigating judges?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the law, they had to have investigating judges. That was the system at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the district military court also have a manner in which complaints could be taken or lodged?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The procedure was identical. I already said that both the civilian court and the military court applied the same procedure. The only difference were the perpetrators, whether they were military or civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So could persons contact the district military prosecutor if they knew of someone committing a crime that came under that jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The law provided the possibility to all individuals and to all institutions or bodies that were mentioned, stipulated, by the law to report various criminal offences. So this was not a possibility, this was also a duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Just for sake of clarity, does that mean that the military police could report incidents to the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. The military police were linked to the military prosecutor, just as the civilian police was linked to the civilian prosecutor. And the prosecutor exerted control over military police, according to our act on criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could military commanders of units or battalions, or at any level, also report crimes directly to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would the same -- could the same be said for a soldier, any military soldier? Could he or she report crimes to the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I already said that any individual could report crimes, including military persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, I'd like to ask, in terms of institutions, could there be referrals from other types of military courts to a district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Various state bodies, military bodies, institutions such as hospitals, civilian defence, any institution or body was entitled and also obliged, according to the Criminal Procedure Act.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, did you assist the Office of the Prosecutor in the past two days to make a diagram illustrating what you have just testified about, the functioning of the district military court system?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have this exhibit handed up, and I believe that there was a manner of attaching it so that the cameras could look at it closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not going to be easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, if I might explain, I understand that there is a technical problem with the computer programmes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And we were unable to place this in Sanction due to the computer programme one makes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I suggest we do, Ms. Sellers, and, Usher, please follow me carefully, I think we need to start referring to this chart bit by bit as we go along, and the usher will try and do her best to follow us. The witness can try to follow on the monitor. The usher will try to follow what we are being shown by -- or what Ms. Sellers wants us to see in this chart, and you try to focus the ELMO on that part. And then we'll move up and down and sideways on the ELMO, according to the indications of Ms. Sellers, and the witness will simply not bother about the ELMO and try to follow on the screen, on the monitor. That's the only way I can see it happening. Otherwise, it's difficult. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may take some time, because it's -- for the usher and us to go straight to the point where you would like us to, it may not be easy. But anyway, let's start.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at your screen. Is it up on there now? I believe this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I have your indulgence for one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: On your screen, could you please describe for the Trial Chamber the diagram we're seeing on the screen in terms of the composition and functioning of the district military court. What does what we're seeing now represent?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: According to the Criminal Procedure Act, there were pre-trial phases of the procedure, when we had investigation carried out by the investigating judge. Following that, there are trial judges who tried in councils or in chambers, consisting of one judge and two jurors, or two professional judges and three jurors for more serious criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to now move the diagram -- yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tankic, the part of the diagram you're looking at now has several lines that appear to link it between this diagram and the one we saw previously. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber the functioning between the district military prosecutor's office and the prior diagram that included the judges, investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: According to the Criminal Procedure Act that was done, in effect, the criminal procedure had to be launched by a prosecutor. The charges were done -- sent to the prosecutor. He would then make an application to the investigating judge to undertake the investigation. Following this, the case was sent back to the prosecutor to determine whether he would launch an indictment or drop the charges. If the indictment was met, then the indictment would be sent to the court for the trial. So this is the procedure in brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that the reason why we see lines that go backward and forward between the district military prosecutor's office and the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I think what I would like to show, we'll just leave it right there, and could you please look to the right of the screen. I believe we have to -- I'm sorry, the other way. You've just taken it off. All right. The square to my right of the district military prosecutor's office, what does that represent, Mr. Tankic?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This is what I spoke about a short while ago, that the information concerning a criminal act could come from these institutions mentioned here, so from civilian police, various institutions, government bodies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could we now move the diagram in the other direction and bring it down, please. I'd like to show the relationship between --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I assist the usher for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Usher, why don't you approach Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will try in the future to have a much more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't blame you for this, Ms. Sellers. It's not easy. I can tell you from past experience that this is not easy. But this is the only way of doing it. The only other way is to have it even blown up further and have it on a board, and then someone will point to it. But, again, we don't have that here. And it's also the -- the process is being made easier because I take it the witness does understand a little bit of English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that makes things easier, because otherwise we would have had further problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, could you please explain, looking now to the left-hand side of the diagram where the military prosecutor is, and explain what those lines and that part of the diagram indicates.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This is the military structure that I'm familiar with from the former JNA, when I served. I'm familiar with the laws and the respective bodies used by the prosecutor in his work, as well as by the investigating judge. You have the military police, the security organ, that is, different levels depending, from a unit level to a staff level. I don't see the disciplinary prosecutor on the screen, and what I can see down here are the special courts that try exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the lines that connect the institutions that you've just testified about, the military police, the security police, the military -- special military court and disciplinary court, what do those lines indicate that run to the district military prosecutor's box in the diagram?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: These lines were drawn under the law. All these bodies are authorised to report a crime to the military prosecutor with jurisdiction over that particular criminal offence. And then, of course, the prosecutor's charges, reports, or approvals are sent to the relevant judge, and this works the other way around too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask you to look at the other part of the diagram. We won't be able to fit it all on, but the other side of the diagram. Mr. Tankic, I want to draw your attention to what is listed here as brigade commander, the little man in green, and ask you, was someone in that position also able to contact the military district prosecutor, and does the chart indicate such?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I. I hate to interrupt, but I'm getting increasingly uncomfortable with this exercise for a number of reasons. Firstly, we've just seen the chart for the first time, so we're trying to get to grips with it as well. It would have been useful to have this as well before the hearing. But the problem, it goes back to what Your Honour was dealing with earlier, that this witness, first of all, isn't an expert witness. If he's confirming provisions of law, then that's one thing; if he's confirming something within his experience, that's another thing, but then we need to be precise about whether it's his experience in the JNA in the former Yugoslavia or experience in this, or -- these may be matters for cross-examination. But my concern is that there are things here, for example, this special military court, where we don't see what the law is which governs the special military court. It hasn't been mentioned in evidence and it's not -- this witness hasn't mentioned in any way how his experience qualifies him to speak about it. I'm also not clear whether he drew up this chart or whether the Prosecution drew it up and he assisted with it. I may be anticipating objections to this chart as an exhibit, matters which I can cross-examine upon. But I do want to state now that we're not happy with this exercise without at least it being clear what laws we're talking about, for example, for this special military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Incidentally, apart from that, which calls for some kind of explanation from you, or at least it could also be in the form of questions to the witness, there is also another matter that I notice as regards -- in relation to these district military courts. There is underlined there "not functional."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the special military court, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, the special military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the extreme left, there is a district military court, "not functional."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness will not be testifying about the special district military court nor about the disciplinary military court. They are there. We intend to use this exhibit with this witness for the knowledge that he has been able to assist us with in terms of the complaint procedure, the structure of the district military court. He has knowledge that one can send complaints from these entities, but the reason that they have not been further described and attention is not drawn to that is that this witness is not, in our opinion, brought forward to give evidence concerning those two institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, you have heard what Mr. Jones said. We are not much wiser or informed on this matter than Mr. Jones is. We only know what we can see on this chart here. So it's -- obviously, it's the case of asking the witness to explain some of these movements to and from one section to the other, because that requires some kind of explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And try to restrict it to what -- I assume that if this was drawn up on the basis of the information that he gave you, then he is in a position to assist us and explain each and every movement that we have here on this chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, he's testified, but he's assisted us in drawing this up. I would say that there was a preliminary diagram, and he has corrected and assisted us in confirming it. We can certainly direct those questions to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're not going to say anything further. You are familiar now, you have heard what Mr. Jones' concerns are, and they seem to be, on the face of it, concerns that carry considerable weight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just might clarify. I don't understand whether Mr. Jones' concerns are a question of weight of the exhibit that he is not objecting when we will be submitting it into evidence, or whether that objection goes to the submission of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm certainly planning to object to the admission of the exhibit for the reason that there are matters here which this witness isn't in a position to help us with, and therefore, if it was admitted as proof of the truth of its contents, that would be wrong because that would be going beyond the scope of what he's testified about. And it's also an objection, really, to the inherently -- inherent suggestiveness or leading nature of questions being put by putting a chart before him which he's only been partially involved in drawing up, and saying, Does it work like this, and the witness saying yes. The evidence is being obtained by suggestion. I would object to the admission of the exhibit, and I will come back to these points in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it's pretty clear what his concerns are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly understand. Let me clarify some of that with questioning to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially this last part he raised, because actually what you are doing is you are presenting -- you are presenting the witness with a nice cake and on the top it's written "nice chocolate cake, baked by," et cetera, and you're asking him to confirm that this is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, did you, when you discussed with the Office of the Prosecutor, look at a chart and therefore -- and then make corrections, changes, any modifications according to your knowledge of how the district military court functioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry again to interrupt. But please do remember that I come from the defence in my career. I would first want to know what you showed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then what he corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In order to be able to come to the conclusion that this is a correct representation of what the witness believes to be the setup or the organisational and procedural setup as regards military justice is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, when you were -- were you presented, during your proofing, with a chart similar to this by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may be allowed to explain. This chart shows a solution under the law on criminal procedure, a solution on how procedures should be conducted before the district military prosecutor. I have very little knowledge about military structures and military issues. This chart only shows legal solutions, and that's all I know about. Nothing else apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you saw this chart in its initial form, did you inform the Office of the Prosecutor where, according to your knowledge of legal issues, that parts of the chart should be modified or changed?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Substantial changes, in fact, have been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did those changes include the relationship between the district military prosecutor and the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did those changes therefore place the investigating judge within the part of the diagram where we see the military court and the judges?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did those changes include the relationship between the civilian sector and the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you inform the Office of the Prosecutor that both civilian police, civilian citizens, and civilian institutions may bring complaints directly to the district military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I insisted that a correction be entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you also make modifications as they relate to the part of the chart that talks about the military security service and the military police, MP?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you say that the changes on the chart that you have made, according to your legal knowledge, render this a chart that describes how the district military court functioned in terms of receiving complaints and conducting investigations in cases?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: That's the only thing the chart actually shows, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I understand that we're close to our break time. I can stop here and will continue afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a preliminary matter, during the break I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Filed all documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank goodness, no, for this witness. But I just realised in the use of the documents that we did find yesterday, I had anticipated to go a bit longer today to discuss certain legal aspects, as I'm sure Your Honours might have noticed within the statutes, and so I believe that this afternoon's session will be curtailed, will be a bit shorter, unless we start the section with the documents. So since we've already conveyed to Defence counsel that is something we'll do tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a problem. If we -- if it's necessary to overflow on to Friday, we can do that without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. I just wanted to inform Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, because I have just been told that the Plenary that was planned for Friday is not going to take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, may I just say that we have, during the break, had an opportunity to look at the documents, and I wouldn't want to stop the Prosecution from moving on to the documents later today. Having looked at them, you know, that's not something which actually has to take place tomorrow. And so certainly for our part, if we could conclude by Thursday, that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday. Mr. Jones and Ms. Sellers, as always, we are at your disposal. So now that you've heard Mr. Jones, perhaps you can proceed and continue today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we'll try and finish with the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe that we were still asking Mr. Tankic certain questions about the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to draw Mr. Tankic's attention to this part of the chart. [Indicates]. Mr. Tankic, would you please look at the indication of a small person in green that says "Commander" under it. Would it be your testimony that the lines, the dotted lines that go from the commander to the other side of the chart, back to the military prosecutor, indicates a means of being able to bring a complaint to the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would this chart also represent that all levels of commanders could bring charges to the district military prosecutor via the military security service or the military police or directly themselves?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Usually this would go through the military police or the security body, but it could go straight to the prosecutor as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the only questions that I wanted to ask this witness concerning the chart. I would now ask if the chart could be given a P number and moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My objection remains, really, just to this chart being -- having any independent probative value. If it's merely as an aid to understanding this witness's testimony, then that's one thing, but we would object to it being -- being considered as having any independent probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please try to position the chart -- let me explain to you, following this route here, this, from the commander on to the district military prosecutor, halfway, there is MP where the journey seems to be interrupted. There is MP and pre-trial duties. You have to look further down. The red -- red dotted line, the red dotted line. There is, at a certain point it goes up and then goes down and continues and that is a chain of connection between the commander, who initiates proceedings and the district military prosecuting officer. Somewhere along the way, there seems to be a stop at the MP. Could the witness please explain to us what MP stands for and, also, I see below that the words "pre-trial duties", what are those pre-trial duties. Let's start from there. What does MP stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Military police, yes. And did the military police have pre-trial duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if a commander -- a commander, as I see it, had these options: First of all, he had to report to the -- to the SVK or to the district military prosecutor. He could suspend the procedure. He could pronounce a disciplinary order, he could decide that he was not authorised to decide and then he would pass it on to his superior, or else he would initiate proceedings and start going down this road to the district military prosecutor. Now, why would he have to stop at the military police? In other words, it seems that, to me, that once he has decided to initiate proceedings, it seems to me, if I try to follow this route, that the first time this journey ends up at the military police office it says: Criminal charge against the armed forces. This is, I assume, in the case of civilians allegedly committing crimes against the armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, in part. The usual procedure to file a criminal report was to file civilian reports with the civilian police and military reports with the military police. They would process the report, gather information and then eventually forward this report to the prosecutor. By way of example, an arrest can only be carried out by the military police in a case like this. However, that does not preclude, as I said at the outset, a complaint from being filed directly with the prosecutor, but they would send it back to the military police for verification before it is eventually decided whether it would be passed on to the military prosecutor, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because I see a further note here which says that for criminal offences against the armed forces, the authorised member of the military police shall file criminal charges to the military prosecutor through his superior officer holding the post of a brigade or division commander or of an equal or higher position, so that you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, would there be any further reason why the decision by the commander, to initiate proceedings, would have to stop at the military police, apart from what we have just discussed or would it go straight to the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could go straight to the military prosecutor -- district military prosecutor. Security organ was a superior body to the military police. Normally, that would be the case. In some way, they have legal jurisdiction over the military police, I mean the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for clarification. At the last point, MP pre-trial duties, the dotted line which leads to MP and goes on, does it mean that it was a clear interruption? Or what does it mean here? If you -- you told us that can it go directly to the military prosecutor. That means that it must not necessarily go via the MP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily, but, Your Honour, there's a problem with the system that was in place at the time. On the one hand we had pre-trial proceedings. We had criminal proceedings and the trial itself. Pre-trial proceedings were carried out in a civilian matter by the civilian police and in a military matter by the military police with their respective jurisdictions, including, for example, an on-site investigation taking photographs of the scene of crime and then gathering potential evidence. This would be the definition of pre-trial proceedings. And then the police might decide to send this on to a prosecutor. However, had they decided straight away that this had to go to the prosecutor, there was nothing standing in their way. And then, if something was still missing, the prosecutor would send the case back to the police, for further processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One further -- one further question. What does the acronym SVK stand for? SVK. It's at the top left, extreme top left. It's a red flag. At the very top. SVK. Is it the commander, or something? Is it the supreme commander, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should look at the entire chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, could you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The immediate superior, the immediate superior. That's what I see. These here are the various military structures which I am not exactly familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Let's leave it at that. Do you have any questions, Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. You answered the question whether it was part of a commander to send a case directly to the military prosecutor. In saying that, I understood it that you meant that when the case reached the military police or the military security service, they could decide to send it immediately on to the military prosecutor. So that would be a decision for the security service, or would it be a decision made by the commander himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, well, this is a question of military subordination. You have to look at the various competencies but I think a commander is superior to all of the services that are under him further down the chain, and therefore any decision that he makes must be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, are you finished with this chart?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to have it given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This will be 498.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This chart is being tendered and received and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P498. And in the various interests that you will prepare, of course, you will make a note that this is being challenged to an extent by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't told us, Ms. Sellers, what do you intend this document to prove?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is, on the one hand, an illustration of oral testimony that has been given. It is an aid to the Trial Chamber in that instance. And we would like to inform both Defence and the Trial Chamber that we will be using this chart with other witnesses so that the oral testimony can have some type of physical representation. But I believe that beyond being an aid, that this chart in itself is also indicative of what the law was at the time, so therefore other exhibits that have been entered into evidence do have a bearing upon how this chart has been designed and what it explains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, the first purpose is fine, but as a representation of the law, unless and until that's elucidated by witnesses, then we would object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have asked you the question, obviously, to have that answer so that it goes on record, in other words, we have the specifics of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's proceed, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, if I could just recall, you testified that the Tuzla district military court started to function in September of 1992. Is that correct?
