utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was it at that time period that the High Court in Tuzla then ceased to hear complaints or to try cases concerning the military personnel that were now picked up by the district military courts' jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. All cases were turned over to the district military court, obviously those cases where perpetrators were military persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you, where were you employed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: In that year I was appointed the chief cantonal prosecutor in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is the chief cantonal prosecutor's office in Tuzla a civilian court or a military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a civilian court, does it resume jurisdiction over cases that concern military members, much as the civilian courts did prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Military courts ceased to operate in 1996, and so immediately after the war, operations ceased and all cases were turned over to relevant courts, either municipal or the cantonal court, depending on where a particular criminal offence was committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The cantonal court that you worked at, starting in 1999, did it receive the materials from the Tuzla district military court upon its secession?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I know that the prosecutor's office received cases from the military prosecution office, and I assumed that the cantonal court did the same, so that it received cases from the district military court in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were the records from the district military prosecutor then kept in a place at the cantonal prosecutor's office where you worked?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Some of the cases, some of the files are still kept in the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were reports written by persons working in the prosecutor's office concerning the contents of the files turned over by the district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I believe that what is in these reports are a number of cases, so when that -- when the files were turned over in 1996, we recorded a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tankic, you started working at that court in 1999. Did you have predecessors who occupied your position as a high prosecutor between 1996 up until 1999, or at a slightly earlier period?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: There were two persons who were my predecessors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Trial Chambers the name of these persons.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Until 1996, Helic Vildana, and between 1997 and 1999, Cane Dzanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to read --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to read reports made by your predecessors concerning materials transferred from the Tuzla district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I had to, since some cases were still active at the time when I came, so the trials were underway. Also, in 2002, we had one decision made. This is why I was acquainted with the cases that were turned over to us from the district military prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In order to clarify, for the record, are you still currently employed at the high cantonal court as a prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Since the 1st of March, I have been the judge of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, have you also had the opportunity to review the archives of the prosecutor's office, in particular to review and see if the materials have arrived from the Tuzla district military court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any cases transferred between the district military prosecutor's office and your office that concerned war crimes committed by Muslim soldiers against Serbs, either civilians or prisoners of war, in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of such cases. I don't believe there was any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If Your Honours would allow me, I would like to specifically ask questions as they relate to our indictment, although the answer that Mr. Tankic has given now might appear to have covered some of the relevant time period and incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed. Take it slowly, bit by bit, and then we'll see. Because if you are simply asking the witness to confirm what he has just stated, I think it will be a useless journey. You know, it's a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he would be stating it just in more specific form as related to specific incidents in the indictment. That's why I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any special objection on your part, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think I can raise any objection, apart from the observation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can be done, although I personally consider it to be a little bit -- anyway, let's proceed and go through it slowly, or not slowly, as quickly as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, to your knowledge, were there any war crimes that would come under Article 142 or 143 or 145 of the code applied to the district military office that were brought by commanders of the Srebrenica army in relation to events that occurred in Jezestica, on August 8th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer, because the question is a little bit different. The judge steps in the whole scenario the moment the sort of jurisdiction of the military courts was transferred over, back to the cantonal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm sorry if I could clarify. I'm asking Mr. Tankic has already testified that he reviewed documents, that he has looked at reports. I'm just asking him to his knowledge within these documents or archival material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has he reviewed archival material related to the period of time when the military tribunals, military courts were in operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour that's what he has testified to. Maybe I should clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better clarify it, be more clear about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tankic, materials that you've testified that were received from the district military prosecutor's office in Tuzla, did they cover the period of 1992 until the court ceased to exist in 1996?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The archives referred to that period and obviously we worked on the cases that were not over, where the decision was still not made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in other words, this archive or archives included also decisions -- cases that had been terminated already before the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you went through those as well, in other words, you are in a position to testify also on those cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously I have not reviewed the entire archives, but I had reports for each year. I read reports for each year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your question now, please, which obviously has to be limited by what the witness has just stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, from the reports of the archives, Mr. Tankic, are you aware of any cases or prosecutions brought by commanders of the Srebrenica army concerning crimes under the jurisdiction of the district military court such as 142 and 143, 144, as concerns, Serb victims in Jezestica, in August 8th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I said at the very beginning that there were no cases concerning war crimes. There were several ordinary crimes that were perpetrated by commanders and they were tried by military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, then I will cease this line of questioning, but I did want to make the record clear that the war crimes that would pertain to acts within our indictment, the witness did not see any of those cases arrive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well if he didn't see any case, I suppose he didn't see any case, which is mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it follows as a logical consequence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tankic, I would like to show you the Prosecution's following exhibit. It is P number 44. Your Honours, it will come in Sanctions in one minute. Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at this document and I would draw your attention to the last sentence in the document. Could you state that the legal institution that's referred to here, military High Court, refers to the jurisdiction that the district military court in Tuzla would have had?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I object to that question. This isn't -- this document is not a document authored by this witness and there's simply a phrase there referring to the military High Court. If this witness is being asked to speculate about what that -- what the author of this document could have meant when he refers to military High Court that would, in my submission, be impermissible and apart from that question I don't see what else he can be asked to help with with this phrase. The document says what it says. Military High Court."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would state that the witness has just testified about his knowledge of the district military court in Tuzla. He has testified about the basis of the jurisdiction, the statute. I have asked him to look at the document. Okay. And then to look at the last sentence and to see whether, from his knowledge, what he knows that this could refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean it's not being put -- the witness was being suggested that he's the author of -- or responsible for what is contained in this document. He's merely being asked a simple question. He's being referred to the last part of that document. And specifically asked whether the -- the military High Court, the jurisdiction of that military High Court basically refers to jurisdiction, that the district military court in Tuzla would have had. I mean, it's -- I think, on the basis of information that he has been providing us, he is perfectly in a position to answer that question. If he is not, he will tell us. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, really the question is, although it says military High Court, could the author have meant to put Tuzla district military court, which I don't see how a witness can be asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- when he is not the author. Secondly, jurisdiction, this document doesn't refer to any jurisdiction, or crimes. So I don't see what jurisdiction he's being -- he's being referred to. We know what the jurisdiction of the Tuzla district military court is. We don't know what the district of the jurisdiction of this military High Court is. And I simply don't see how there's an intelligible question which this witness can be asked about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I basically see nothing objectionable in the question that has been put. He is being asked to explain whether military High Court that is mentioned in this last part of this document is basically tantamount to the Tuzla military district -- Tuzla district military or the jurisdiction that court would have had. I think it's a harmless question and perfectly legitimate. So if you can answer it -- if you can, because if you -- you can't, obviously tell us you can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was created by the security body, security service, as far as I can see, and they really used wrong information here. The military law encompassed military court and military prosecution and here they should have mentioned military prosecution, that was the only institution that existed at the time. There were no other courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that answer, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we move --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I just want to stay with the document again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Tankic, in looking at the document, would the types of criminal responsibility, as referred to in the third paragraph of this document, come under the jurisdiction of the Tuzla military district court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: It should have been estimated at the time by the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Was the district military prosecutor functioning at the date that this document has in its letterhead?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, is that the Tuzla district?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, you might answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It existed since September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would persons who -- excuse me, I'll just with draw that question. Do you have any knowledge, Mr. Tankic, of what is written at the top of the document, "The Summary Court Martial of Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I heard that from films, from movies, "summary court martial". But according to our law, we did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tankic, are you familiar with what is written underneath that, "The Commission for Mediation with the Enemy"?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The BH Presidency established a commission for exchange of prisoners. That is the commission that I am familiar with. Maybe this is meant to be the same one, I really don't know. But certainly this formulation is very awkward.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is already into evidence. I would just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness the next exhibit, which is P46.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at the last paragraph of this document, please. And would this be the type of incidents that would come under the jurisdiction of the Tuzla military district court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Various allegations are described here and it was up to the prosecutor to determine whether he wanted to continue with the procedure, or not. If the person was only arrested, then, no. But there are also certain suspicions here which can be further investigated by the prosecution, by the district military prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like the witness to see the following exhibit. It is P486. And I'm only referring to the first page of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sellers, my attention is being drawn that this document is under seal, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, there has been no indication to the witness concerning some things in the document and names are not to be mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you intend to use the first page, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would just like to ask the witness whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the pages are not in sequence. In other words, if you see the last three digits, one has 195, the other one is 613, the other one is 145. So perhaps you could tell me -- could tell us straight away, first and foremost, which is the first page of the three.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That would be 195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 195. One moment. Let me read it and try to remember why it is ... Can anyone remind me why it was put under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see. I see. That's why. So how do -- now I think you've lost your chance --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask you to withdraw your question before I answer it next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can, because it's partly my fault I led you into this blind alley, we could photocopy this first page now and then cancel, all right, the first line or the first -- well, what -- what is the purpose -- what do you want to prove?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The purpose of this, Your Honour, would be the contrast with the previous documents that we've sent -- that we've shown the witness, in terms of choices to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you need the witness to show us the contrast?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can ask him directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, you can actually make reference later on at the right moment when it comes to submissions --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to this document, and the contrast, if there is one at all, will emerge.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's the way to proceed at this point. And my apologies to you if I actually tricked you into being unable to put the question, but please do remember that I come from the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, with the preceding documents that we have seen that made reference to a high court, I would like to ask you: Have you, in looking through the archives and the reports of the prosecutor's office in Tuzla, high cantonal office, as of 1999, did you see any of these cases related to these individuals come within the archives?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Nothing whatsoever in the documents that I went through, but as I've told you, I didn't go through all the individual cases in detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything in the reports related to the cases that ever included information of prosecutions or initiations concerning the individuals or the types of individuals in the documents I've just shown you?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Nothing that I could see based on the Srebrenica prosecutor's reports, or the Tuzla prosecutor's reports for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move to a different area now. After September 1992 and until the spring of 1993, to your knowledge were there any civilian prosecutors in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I know about civilian judicial bodies in Srebrenica based on the prosecutors' and court presidents' reports. I know it was sent up in Srebrenica on the 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please inform us whether the prosecutor's office set up in June 1993 handled cases that were first instant cases or cases that were cases that were major cases?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This was a basic prosecutor's office and a basic court, first instance court in Srebrenica. They could handle cases with a sentence of up to 10 years, from the moment they were established. Furthermore, the law that had been adopted from the former Yugoslavia provided for a possibility that in certain cases they carry out investigations on account of urgency and then hand the case over to the higher court or prosecutor. Under the law then in force, all they could handle were crimes with a sentence of up to 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the person who was the civilian prosecutor as of June of 1993 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know her personally, but her name was familiar from reports. The name was Dzuzida Akagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And have you read reports that have either spoken about her and her work or that she herself has authored?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I read reports that she produced. I also read reports drawn up by the higher prosecutor. This was produced back in 1995 when the lady prosecutor fled Srebrenica, which was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber the name of the person that Ms. Akagic reported to? Who was her superior?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Who was Akagic's superior, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: At this time, High Prosecutor Vildana Helic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is that the same person who was one of your predecessors that you currently -- that you held up until March 1999?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This person remained in her position throughout the war until 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, in reading over the reports concerning the civilian prosecutor's office in Srebrenica, would you be able to state whether criminal activity was pursued, charges raised, and trials conducted?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Reports were produced in a highly professional manner. You can draw conclusions based on that and realise what the judiciary was like in Srebrenica at that time. Prosecutor Akagic submitted reports on her own work back in 1994 -- 1993, 1994, and as for the first six months of 1995, she gave an oral presentation to the higher prosecutor in person, having been expelled from Srebrenica. If you look at these reports, you realise that she took steps to prosecute crimes. You can clearly discern the sort of criminal offences that she dealt with. For example, in a 1993 report, there is reference to about 40 cases, that's between the first of June 1993 and the end of that year, there were murders, aggravated theft, theft, infanticide, as far as I remember, crimes of a more general nature, if I can call it that. Once she submitted this report, she asked the high prosecutor to tell her what to do about the cases which she had no jurisdiction over, namely serious crimes requiring a sentence of over 10 years. The Tuzla-based high prosecutor took steps in cooperation with the president of the High Court and submitted a report to the Ministry of Justice in Sarajevo. Subsequently, the minister himself decided to grant authority to the Srebrenica prosecutor as of the 1st of April -- as of first of January 1994 to prosecute cases that would normally have fallen under the jurisdiction of the higher prosecutor in Tuzla. This decision was submitted to the Srebrenica prosecutor in January 1994. If you look at her reports, about her activities in 1994, you can clearly see that she acted accordingly. What she emphasised in that particular report was that cases would usually go as far as pressing charges and publishing indictments and hardly ever tried. Most of the cases that were eventually tried were misappropriation of land and crimes dealing with forestry related offences. The next problem that came up had to do with members of the army. She did not have authority over these matters, except where urgent investigations were required. Nevertheless, she was under an obligation to refer all of these cases to the higher district military prosecutor in Tuzla. Srebrenica was besieged at the time. There were no roads that one could use to travel outside Srebrenica, so many cases were stuck in Srebrenica and no further steps were taken. As far as I remember, by 1995, as few as six cases involving murder had been referred to the district military prosecutor. I also know that in 1993 another case was referred to the district military prosecutor and the suspect was handed over. This was a case of triple murder. This case was tried and completed before a military court in Tuzla in 1994. Now, one thing I really don't know is how this case was referred, which method was used to turn the case over. And how the suspect was actually handed over. I have no knowledge or information concerning that. As for all of these reports, from 1993 and 1994, the prosecutor sent these by radio communication and that's how the -- all the replies from the higher prosecutor arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tankic, thank you. I want to go back to some of the points that you have brought up. You testified that the prosecutor in Srebrenica actually asked to have her jurisdiction expanded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When she submitted the 1993 report, she sent a query to the higher prosecutor asking what to do with those cases that she had no jurisdiction over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was her jurisdiction eventually expanded?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice in Sarajevo took a decision in January 1994 to expand her jurisdiction thereby authorising her to take steps that would normally fall under the jurisdiction of a higher military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the expansion of her jurisdiction, in any way, affect military members or civilians related to the military?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: She had no jurisdiction over those matters. Her jurisdiction was never expanded to those areas. This would have fallen under the sole jurisdiction of the military prosecutor. She could only initiate urgent investigations. That was as far as it went. Investigations. That was as far as it went, where there was a danger that something would fall under a statute of limitations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you please explain to the Trial Chamber who had the ability to refer cases to the civilian prosecutor in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: By way of an example, back in 1993 most criminal reports were filed by the public security station in Srebrenica. The total number was 144. 142 of these were filed by the Srebrenica public securities station and the remaining two by civilians who had sustained damage. Needless to say, criminal reports could have been filed by other bodies too. For example, if there had been a military police presence in Srebrenica, they would have been authorised to file a criminal complaint too; someone associated with their security, the commander himself. What I'm telling you now is exactly what the law says on the matter. If you look at her report, you can see who specifically filed these criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tankic, could you also explain that you testified that communications was difficult, but that the Srebrenica prosecutor did send reports in cases to her superior. Would you explain to the Trial Chamber how that was done.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: It's not that communication was difficult. There was no communication. Everything was blocked. Reports were usually sent by radio or telegram using the military -- using the assistance of military bodies, usually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now when you state that reports were sent by radio, was that dependent upon electricity or any other type of physical device that communicated directly between Srebrenica and let's say for example Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I'm not very good with equipment and the technical aspects of communication. I only know that reports were received by radio. In Tuzla, they sometimes had electricity, on and off. The military, in fact, had it from time to time but the civilians had none whatsoever. I'm not sure what the situation was in Srebrenica though.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In terms of telegrams, how were telegrams able to be sent from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: By radio -- radio devices were used. This would normally be coded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show the witness a further exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like the witness to look at the exhibit with ERN number 03648866. Mr. Tankic, are you familiar with this type of apparatus?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: From the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you, please, explain to the Trial Chamber why -- what it is and why you're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA. I was in a reconnaissance unit and we had a radio communications officer who carried a device like this on his back. I think the name of this piece of equipment was RUP20. But I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is this the type of radio equipment that could have been used by the Srebrenica prosecutor to send information out of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If he knows. If he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are in the realm of pure speculation here. I mean, how would he know in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, only because he will have seen the incoming messages and reports that would come from certain types of apparatuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But they would be received coded and then they have to be decoded and that's what he will see. He won't see anything else. I mean it's ... anyway, I mean I won't obstruct you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, are you familiar with the apparatus in ERN number 03648865?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I said that I was, but I'm not sure how it works. When I said that reports were coded, that was just my conclusion. There was a code and a telegram number in the heading, so that was an assumption I made, that these had been coded. I know, however, that these are the sort of radio devices used in the former JNA, but that's about all I know. I can't tell you anything about the way they are operated, or their range or how the actual code is used. I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Tankic, are these wireless devices?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Well, if they were using radio waves, then I suppose they should be wireless, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so, otherwise you would have taken us back to, I don't know, how many years ago. Ms. Sellers, do you intend to tender these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Together or separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: They can be tendered maybe separately, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the first one that we saw, the one ending with the ERN 866, will be P499, and the one with PR -- with -- not PRN, sorry, with ERN 865 will be P500.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only question I would ask the witness on these two pieces of equipment that you saw here: Are you aware if, during the war, this type of equipment was in use? If you are aware, tell us, Yes, I know they were still in use; no, I don't know. Because, after all, these are old JNA equipment. They may have been superseded by more modern equipment at the time. So if you know the answer, give it to us. If you don't, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what type of equipment was used. I didn't see it during the war, not once did I see the actual system that was being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to a different area, given the time period we have to start the second -- the subsequent section after the break, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Absolutely no problem. We'll have a 25-minute break, and then you take it up from there and we'll finish at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or at whatever time is convenient for you, considering obviously the areas you will be touching upon. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this next part I would like to ask Mr. Tankic several questions about documents, and we would like to hand those documents up. I just want to explain beforehand that the documents that were related to the attachments to the statement are in one pile that we will indicate which ERN number to look at, and any the other documents, which were the documents relating to yesterday 's adjournment, are separated out. But we would like to hand them up together so that people will be able to look at both sets when appropriate. Furthermore, I've been informed that we will be using a combination of ELMO and Sanction. We were not able to place everything in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate all your efforts today to make things easy, Ms. Sellers. And incidentally, I switched off my -- I must have hit something here. Okay, leave it, I can follow from here. This is gone completely, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, I just saw it saving. I didn't touch anything, but... Yours too. Oh, I see, so it's not just me, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness see the document with ERN number 03648896. I would like to hand these up to the usher, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I don't see 0364 in the bundle that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Tankic, are you familiar with this document that is before you?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Trial Chamber, where did you see this document prior -- let me rephrase that. Did you see this document in your capacity of work as a high prosecutor, in the cantonal court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I ask the usher, have we placed that on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, can you tell us, who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Basic public prosecutor from Srebrenica, Mrs. Dzuzida Akagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the contents, the reason that this document was written?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This is a usual annual report on the work that is submitted directly to the higher prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would the higher prosecutor be Ms. Helic, who you mentioned before, you testified about before?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, looking at the heading on the document, would you please confirm, if you know, how this document was transferred between Srebrenica to Ms. Helic in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: It arrived by radio connection or by telegram through the military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to the first paragraph of this document, would it be your understanding that from around April 1992, the beginning of the war, until the end of December 1993, that it recounts that 35 criminal reports and four other reports concerned the Srebrenica prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is how much she had between the 1st of June, 1993, and the end of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. I don't know who is going to answer that, but this document in its original form, in the B/C/S form, contains four pages, three of which are handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that part of the first page or are they separate pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to ask the witness. Those are the pages, the back pages, that I will ask the witness is he familiar with, what is written on those separate pages you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because you have asked the witness whether this document -- how was this document transmitted, and I can understand the first page being transmitted by telegram, but I can't understand -- or by radio, but I can't understand the second page and the third page and the fourth page being transmitted by radio and therefore only handwriting, or by telegram. I mean, the first one is self-explanatory because there is "Telegram" on the right-hand corner, top right-hand corner, but the other three couldn't have been transmitted by telegram or by radio in the form that they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, did you have the original of this document within your possession or in the archives of the cantonal court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: I found it in the archives of the prosecution office.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And if you would look at the subsequent pages that appear to have handwriting on them, could you inform the Trial Chamber whose handwriting that is.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: The first one is mine. This is to certify that the copy is the same as the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was a copy then made of your original?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is what Your Honours and the defence and Prosecution are looking at now, a copy of your original document and attached is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For sake of clarity, were the pages that included your handwriting part of this original telegram?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would turn your attention back to the document and, particularly, in the last paragraph of the document, would it be your testimony that the prosecutor from Srebrenica, due to war circumstances, had to be flexible at times in the exercise of her duty as it pertained to juveniles?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Earlier in my testimony, I described exactly this what I derived from this report, that the circumstances of work were very difficult, just as the prosecutor described in this report. And criminal cases, mostly seized with pressing of charges or publishing of indictment due to the lack of expert witnesses and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does it appear, from looking at this document, that the prosecutor in Srebrenica nevertheless tried to perform her duties as competently as possible?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, under the given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the document be given a P number and be submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be given P501.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay, the next document has ERN number 03648900. I believe it's in Sanctions -- English version. I would ask Mr. Tankic to look at the document and tell the Trial Chamber, did he possess -- whether he possessed the original of this document and that he handed it over to the Office of the Prosecutor during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had it in my possession and I gave it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And this document represents a copy of the original document that you handed over?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask you to look at the first page with the writing on it, the typed writing. Mr. Tankic when you look at this page, would you please confirm whether this document was transferred between the Srebrenica prosecutor's office to the senior prosecutor's office in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. This is the request that I explained earlier where the prosecutor asked the higher prosecutor for instructions on what to do with the cases that do not fall under her jurisdiction. This is an example of a murder that a higher court had jurisdiction over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you be able to state whether, as a prosecutor, that this was certainly a professional attitude to take, to see what you should do with cases that didn't completely fall under your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was faced with this legal problem of the lack of jurisdiction over such a case, and she had to ask the higher prosecutor what to do with cases of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does the document indicate the manner in which it was transferred between Srebrenica and the senior prosecutor's office in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: In the same way which -- as the previous document, by radio or telegram means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, do you know where in Srebrenica the prosecutor's office was?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: From the prosecutor's reports coming out of Srebrenica, I realise that from the 1st of June, the office of the prosecutor was based in the municipality building of Srebrenica and then, in 1995, it was moved into just one room of the former court house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for a number for this document and to move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So this will be 502.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The next document I understand will be placed on the ELMO. It is ERN number 03648886.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are these the documents that were in dispute, or not? Or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I don't believe there's any dispute about the documents Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: These were certainly the documents that were the subject of our earlier discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That were in dispute. So these are the ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Proceed now. Thank you. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at the document before you and could you once again confirm to the Trial Chamber that the handwriting on the back of the typed pages are your handwriting; that would be -- I don't believe he can see that from the ELMO. I think you would have to show that.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature and the dates written by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And once again, it's because you gave these originals to the Office of the Prosecutor and they made copies from the originals?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, Mr. Tankic, you testified earlier that the Srebrenica prosecutor asked that her jurisdiction be expanded precisely to be able to take on some duties due to the difficulty of wartime. If you look at this document, would you please tell me whether this document is related, in any way, to that request.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This is a response to her request, so this is a response by the higher prosecutor, informing the prosecutor in Srebrenica that the measures were undertaken to extend the jurisdiction of the basic prosecution office in Srebrenica so that they could also handle the cases falling under higher jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at the second page of the document, the one that has ERN number that ends with 888. Now, to your knowledge, was the reason that the increased jurisdiction was requested was because of the physical separation between the senior prosecutor's office and the higher court in Tuzla, and the communication breakdown?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would it be your understanding that the Srebrenica prosecutor's reaction to the difficulties of the war situation, was to, in essence, increase her ability to function well, as opposed to release or to remove herself from her function?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously she made a very professional move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this document be given a P number and submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be 503, P503.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The next document will be in Sanctions. It is ERN number 03648868.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I will ask, for the sake of the record, the same question: Is that your handwriting on the back of page with ERN number 03648869?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are numbers written by me and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does that indicate that you possessed an original copy of this document and that the prosecutor subsequently made a copy from that?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you turn your attention now back to the front of the document. I would ask you to look at the lower part of the document that begins with the title "Decision". It had taken an official decision for the jurisdiction of the Srebrenica prosecutor to be expanded.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the decision by the minister of justice and public administration in Sarajevo, and this decision was published also in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are those the proper legal steps to take when a jurisdiction is ultimately modified, including expanded, of a municipal court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this also be given a P number and ask that it be submitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be P504.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, in other words, if I may add something to the last question and answer. Do I take it that, in those circumstances, as they pertained in January of 1994, it was the executive that had the power to expand, or define actually, the jurisdiction of a public prosecutor's office, a particular public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the time executive powers, especially the Ministry of Justice, were in contact with the prosecution office. Nowadays the prosecution office has total independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to move to a document that is within the annex. 03615766 is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, I ask you to look at this document. Does this document confirm that the prosecutor in Srebrenica was informed by her superior of the expansion of her jurisdiction in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This decision was sent to the prosecution in Srebrenica, and this is the decision on the expansion of her jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If you would look at the document in the upper right-hand side, does it convey the manner in which it was communicated to the Srebrenica prosecutor from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: According to this number, I understand that this was also communicated by radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this be given a P number and submitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The entire bundle, or just this page?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The annex, Your Honour, I think we'll wait until we're finished, although, yes, we'll have the entire annex -- we'll ask for the entire annex to be given a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this will be P505.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, for the record, the previous question -- one moment, because now I've lost it. Yes. The previous question related to the document which is -- the English version is found on page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at the document with ERN number 03615767. This is also in the annex. Page 15. Mr. Tankic, could you please look at this document and inform the Trial Chamber, who is the person, and the function that the person who signed this document holds.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by the Minister of Justice and Administration in Sarajevo, Mr. Kasim Trnka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does this document refer to the expansion of the jurisdiction of the public prosecutor's office in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think there is something wrong, somewhere. I heard you say, Ms. Sellers, that the document you were -- you wanted to address to the witness or wanted the witness to address to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Could you permit me one minute. I understand now what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your assistant actually mentioned page 15, which is correct. That's page 15, the corresponding page in the English text. But the document that we have on page 15 and the corresponding document in the B/C/S with that number are not the same. The one which is in B/C/S, indeed, you have a decision dated the 12th of January, 1994, by the minister, Professor Kasim Trnka. This is what I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the English version, if you look at the bottom of page -- oh, I see it's page 14, all right, page 14. That explains it. The mistake was directing us to page 15. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So if we look at page 14 and 15, because I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- I unfortunately don't have the annex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it, because the one on page 15 was different, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honour, could you just give me one second so I can exactly see what you have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the English version, I would now draw your attention to the top of page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Tankic to look at the document and ask him whether this decision, from the appearance of the document, was it circulated to the district military prosecutor's office in Tuzla, the command of the 28th Division of the Bosnian army in the military security department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt, Ms. Sellers, but that's -- if you look at the B/C/S, what you've just mentioned does not appear on the document which is at page 5767, but it appears on a completely different document, supposedly signed by Alis Sarihodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just withdraw this document for the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's up to you. I mean, I will not involve myself in that, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a different document, definitely. But this is not the decision of the minister. The question was, is it right that this ministerial decision was communicated to, et cetera. What you were referring to is a different ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand that. I would like to withdraw this document, possibly to raise it at a different time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. You can leave it there and raise it at a different time in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. Then can I ask for a P number for it, for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The document, I think we have already given this document, the entire bundle, a number, 505.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later on, if you want to make use of several -- of different parts of this document, you will refer to the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the document number for the entire bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. I would then just like to withdraw my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's up to you. I will not interfere with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to move to document with the ERN number 03648880. Mr. Tankic, I would ask you to look at this document and ask you, are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does this refer to one of the reports that you testified about earlier?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This is a document where the 1994 report of the Srebrenica prosecutor was submitted or forwarded to the public prosecutor in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether this document was submitted while the public prosecutor was in Srebrenica, or was she in a different location at this time?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: While she was still in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know how this document was forwarded?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This fist document was sent to Sarajevo by the higher military prosecutor in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that the record has reflected the ERN number incorrectly and I would just like to state that the ERN number should be 03648880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, did you read the report that was -- from 1994 that was sent to the senior public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Can I now ask that this be moved into evidence with a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be P506.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to go to document ERN number 03648882. It's P506.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, could you please look at this document. Is this document the report from 1994 that our previous exhibit referred to?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you look at the first paragraph of the document and I draw your attention to the last sentence in the first paragraph. Did that indicate that cases were submitted to a military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is reference to the six cases that were submitted to the Tuzla military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would that be the district military prosecutor's office in Tuzla that you testified about earlier?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did the Srebrenica prosecutor, within her function, at times refer cases to the district military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: This report indicates that she only managed to refer these six cases and not any others although they, too, were under the jurisdiction of the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was that within keeping of her function to refer cases to the district military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: It was within keeping of her legal obligations. The military court or prosecutor had sole jurisdiction over military persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In referring cases to the district military court, would it be, from your reading, your knowledge of the documents, concerning crimes committed by military members who were geographically in Srebrenica town or municipality? Or Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is about crimes committed in that area and about serious crimes and I see that's why the prosecutor did these because these were cases of detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour I would ask that this document also be given a P number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It has already been given a number. It is 506.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I am at a deficit because I don't know the difference between the documents in the annex and the others. Excuse me for being repetitious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question to the witness on this particular page that you were being referred to. Just below the six names that were referred to the military court, there are two lines, it starts with "ostale predmete" and next line ends with the words "iz objektivnih razloga", in other words, because of objective reasons. What do you understand by objective reasons? I mean it says that "we have been unable to submit the other cases from 1994 and 1993 to the county military prosecutor's office because of the objective reasons." What would be the objective reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Communication break down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that we have it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Might I just continue where Your Honour's question -- when you look at the crimes that were reported in 1994 or that pertained to the military, do you see any crimes that would be considered war crimes, such as those that we discussed earlier under the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Here where the crimes are described, there is nothing that indicates the existence of any war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Tankic, was there a statute of limitation on the war crimes that came under Article 141 through 145 within the penal code?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: There is no statute of limitations for war crimes and this is under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could war crimes that were committed in 1992 therefore have been prosecuted in 1993, 1994, 1995 or 1996 by the Tuzla military district court?

utterances.speaker: IZO TANKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1996, by the district military court and nowadays by the cantonal court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I do not know whether you want to break at this time, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're asking me. It's up to you. I said before we are here at your disposal and you choose the time when you would like to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I was thinking in terms of the interpreters or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's our time lapse at 7 o'clock, but if you prefer to stop here and then start with something new tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I realise now this will go into tomorrow a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then we'll will stop now provided we try to keep to the schedule -- time schedule that we agreed upon or seem to have agreed upon making it possible for Mr. Jones to conclude tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I hope to go no longer than possibly a half hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So would that be practical for you, to -- for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely, I will certainly be able to finish by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So we will finish here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There is one matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the absence of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, preferably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So I apologise to you for not having addressed you as judge in the beginning, but to my knowledge you are still chief prosecutor. So I address you as judge now. You are going to be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher. We will see you again tomorrow morning when we hope to continue and finish with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter that doesn't concern this witness and in fact to a certain extent it is addressed to the registry but I wanted to mention it in court. I understand my client is actually having to spend a very lengthy period of time here at the Tribunal after the end of the sitting. And if there is any way that that problem could be solved because I understand it is even a matter of hours that he's kept here waiting at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But does it happen when it is an afternoon sitting or does it happen when it is a morning sitting, because from my experience it happens when it is a morning sitting, not when it is a afternoon sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand it certainly happened on Monday and we had an afternoon sitting. Let me just take instructions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I understand it is a general problem related to the quantity of accused here at the Tribunal, that they're all kept waiting together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I know of the existence of that problem, which however makes it obvious that it's not just your client's problem. It's everybody else's problem. One is made to wait for the other. I can't promise you anything, Mr. Jones. What I can promise is you, as I did in other cases, and as I do in other cases, I will do my level best to see whether there could be a solution to this. I can tell you that on previous occasions, when I intervened, I could understand the -- that there is a problem, a logistical problem also because the transportation has been -- has to be coordinated between this Tribunal and the Dutch authorities. It's not just this Tribunal. So I will do my best. I will do my best, but I can't promise you anything, because you understand that the exigencies of the Dutch authorities, this Tribunal, and those of security in general have to be observed. And as the number of cases being heard simultaneously increases, it becomes so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful to Your Honour for any assistance and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll definitely do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- and I raise it as a matter for the Chamber because I suppose, really, it's important for us also, apart from the general well-being of our client, for him to be well rested and in a fair state of mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I fully agree. I fully agree, especially if it's like today and tomorrow where we have sitting in the afternoon today and a sitting in the morning tomorrow, and he will be rushed to dinner, and so on and so forth. So I can assure you, I know of the problem. It's not easy to solve, but I can also tell you that the authorities do their level best, that much I can assure you of. Sometimes it doesn't work. I mean, it's just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm very much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of March, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25
